concept_mcqs.stem:
You receive a new motherboard whose manual shows these CPU power connectors:
```text
Power Connectors
- ATX_24PIN (required)
- ATX_12V_8PIN (required)
- ATX_12V_4PIN (optional, for extreme overclocking)
```
Your PSU cables are:
```text
- 1x 24-pin ATX
- 1x 4+4-pin EPS12V (CPU)
- 2x 6+2-pin PCIe (GPU)
```
The GPU requires two 8‑pin PCIe. Choose the routing that powers the CPU safely without misusing connectors.
options: Use one 6+2‑pin PCIe into the ATX_12V_8PIN and the 4+4 EPS into the optional 4‑pin.
Use the 4+4‑pin EPS joined as 8‑pin into ATX_12V_8PIN, leave the optional 4‑pin empty, and use both 6+2 for the GPU.
Split the 4+4 EPS: put one 4‑pin into ATX_12V_4PIN and the other 4‑pin into one of the GPU sockets.
Use a dual‑6+2 to 8‑pin adapter to feed the CPU 8‑pin; reserve the 4+4 EPS for the GPU.
concept_mcqs.explanation: CPU 8‑pin must be fed by an EPS12V cable. The single 4+4 EPS forms the required 8‑pin for ATX_12V_8PIN. The optional 4‑pin can be left empty. The two 6+2 PCIe are reserved for the GPU.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: PCIe 6+2 is not EPS; pinout and keying differ and can damage hardware. C: Splitting the EPS leaves neither device properly powered; GPUs do not accept EPS halves. D: Adapters from PCIe to EPS are improper; CPU power should come from native EPS12V.

concept_mcqs.stem:
ESD audit of a bench shows:
```text
Wrist strap tester (loop): 0.9 MΩ PASS
Mat surface resistance (Rs): 7.0 x 10^7 Ω (PASS)
Mat resistance-to-ground (Rtg): OPEN (FAIL)
Relative humidity: 22%
Mat ground cord continuity to CPC: FAIL
```
Per ANSI/ESD S20.20, which single change FIRST brings the workstation back into compliance?
options: Increase humidity to 45–55% to reduce resistance.
Attach the mat’s ground cord to a verified common point ground (CPC) and retest Rtg.
Replace the wrist strap because the tester reading is close to 1 MΩ.
Turn off nearby bench power supplies to reduce leakage currents.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The failing parameter is Rtg (mat not bonded to ground). Restoring the ground connection to a verified CPC immediately brings the workstation within spec given the passing surface resistance and strap.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Humidity may help surface resistance, but Rs already passes; Rtg remains OPEN without a ground bond. C: The strap already passes; replacing it does not correct the mat ground failure. D: Bench PSUs don’t fix a missing ground connection.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After installing a 240 mm AIO, the system thermal throttles within 60 seconds. BIOS Hardware Monitor shows:
```text
CPU Temp: 98°C (rising)
CPU_FAN: 1900 RPM (radiator fan splitter)
AIO_PUMP: 0 RPM
CHA_FAN1: 2600 RPM
```
Pump cable is currently on CHA_FAN1, radiator fan splitter on CPU_FAN. Which change yields stable cooling and a clean POST (no fan errors)?
options: Leave wiring as is; set CPU_FAN to Full Speed and CHA_FAN1 to Silent.
Disable CPU Fan Monitoring in BIOS to avoid the error; cooling will normalize under load.
Move pump to AIO_PUMP header and set its control to 100% (DC/PWM), keep radiator fans on CPU_FAN with curve.
Move radiator fans to AIO_PUMP and pump to CPU_FAN so BIOS tracks pump speed.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The pump must run at constant full speed from AIO_PUMP, and radiator fans should be on CPU_FAN with an appropriate curve. That restores flow and proper monitoring.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Full speed CPU_FAN does not power the pump; pump on CHA_FAN1 may still be voltage/curve limited. C: Putting fans on AIO_PUMP removes useful CPU‑based control; pump on CPU_FAN may not run full‑time. D: Hiding the error doesn’t fix zero pump RPM; overheating persists.

concept_mcqs.stem:
On first boot, an ASUS board shows Q‑LEDs cycling CPU→DRAM, then VGA LED stays solid. Monitor is black. Build notes:
```text
CPU: Ryzen 5 3600 (no iGPU)
GPU: RTX 3070, two 8‑pin sockets
GPU Power: none connected yet
Monitor cable: HDMI to motherboard rear I/O
```
What action will resolve the no‑display condition?
options: Remove one RAM stick to reduce training time.
Connect the case front‑panel HD Audio header.
Enable CSM in BIOS to support the GPU.
Move the HDMI cable to the GPU and connect both GPU 8‑pin PCIe power leads.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The CPU lacks integrated graphics, so video must come from the discrete GPU, which also needs its PCIe power. Plug the monitor into the GPU and power the card.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: CSM choice doesn’t matter if the GPU is unpowered and the monitor is on the motherboard. C: RAM count doesn’t fix missing GPU power or wrong display output. D: HD Audio is unrelated to video initialization.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You install 4×16 GB DDR4‑3600 (dual‑rank) on a board whose manual states:
```text
Memory Support (Ryzen 3000 IMC)
- 2 DIMMs: up to 3600 MT/s (OC)
- 4 DIMMs (dual‑rank): 2666–2933 MT/s typical, CR=2T recommended
```
POST fails with DRAM LED lit when XMP 3600 is enabled. Which BIOS memory setup is most likely to POST and run stably?
options: Set JEDEC 2133 CL15 at 1.20 V, CR=1T.
Increase DRAM voltage to 1.50 V and keep 3600 MT/s.
Manually set 2933 MT/s, DRAM 1.35 V, SOC +0.02 V, CR=2T.
Enable XMP 3600, leave all else Auto.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With four dual‑rank DIMMs, the IMC typically tops out around 2666–2933. Using 2933 with modest voltage and 2T command rate aligns with the manual’s guidance and usually POSTs.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: XMP 3600 often fails with 4× dual‑rank. B: 2133 will POST but leaves significant, unnecessary performance on the table; the question asks what is most likely stable at reasonable speed. D: 1.50 V is excessive for standard DDR4 and risks damage; frequency is still too high for 4× dual‑rank.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You need the HDD activity LED working. The front‑panel header from the manual:
```text
Front Panel Header (F_PANEL)
Pins (odd top row L→R): 1 3 5 7 9
Pins (even bottom row L→R): 2 4 6 8 10
1: HDD_LED_P   3: HDD_LED_N   5: RESET_SW_P   7: RESET_SW_N   9: +5V (key)
2: PWR_LED_P   4: PWR_LED_N   6: PWR_SW_P     8: PWR_SW_N     10: NC
Case leads: HDD LED (+/-), PWR LED (+/-), PWR SW, RESET SW
```
Which placement and polarity makes the HDD LED function?
options: Place HDD LED leads on pins 1(+),3(−).
Place HDD LED leads on pins 2(+),4(−).
Place HDD LED leads on pins 3(+),1(−).
Place HDD LED leads on pins 6(+),8(−).
concept_mcqs.explanation: Per the pinout, HDD LED uses pins 1 (positive) and 3 (negative). Placing the leads there with correct polarity illuminates on disk activity.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Pins 2/4 are the Power LED. C: Pins 6/8 are the Power Switch. D: Reversed polarity on pins 1/3 prevents a diode LED from lighting.

concept_mcqs.stem:
BIOS shows the NVMe drive under NVMe Information, but Boot Option Priorities lists only SATA devices. Current settings:
```text
Boot -> CSM: Enabled (Legacy & UEFI)
Secure Boot: Disabled
SATA Mode: AHCI
NVMe Info: Samsung 980 PRO 1TB (Detected)
```
Without installing any OS, which firmware change makes the NVMe drive eligible as a boot target?
options: Switch SATA Mode to RAID.
Initialize the NVMe drive with an MBR partition table.
Force PCIe slots to Gen3 instead of Auto.
Disable CSM (UEFI only) and set OS Type to Windows UEFI Mode.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Many boards only expose NVMe boot options in pure UEFI mode. Disabling CSM enables NVMe boot path enumeration.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: SATA mode doesn’t affect NVMe boot enumeration. B: Link speed rarely controls whether NVMe appears as bootable. D: MBR vs GPT matters to bootloaders, not to the firmware’s decision to list an NVMe device before any OS is installed.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Power budgeting before first boot:
```text
CPU: 125 W (peaks 160 W)
GPU: 320 W (transients up to 2x for milliseconds)
Motherboard, drives, fans: 60 W
Total steady: ~505 W
```
Which PSU choice best avoids OCP trips during GPU transients while providing headroom?
options: 650 W PSU, single 12 V rail @ 54 A
650 W PSU, dual 12 V rails @ 18 A each for PCIe outputs
450 W PSU, single 12 V rail @ 34 A
550 W PSU, single 12 V rail @ 40 A
concept_mcqs.explanation: A quality 650 W unit with a strong single 12 V rail (~54 A) provides sufficient steady power and transient headroom without tripping per‑rail OCP during GPU spikes.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/B: Insufficient 12 V current headroom for 500+ W steady and spikes. D: Two 18 A rails (216 W each) on PCIe may trip during GPU transients.

concept_mcqs.stem: You must install a Ryzen 5 5600 on a B450 board with stickered BIOS v1201. CPU support list says v2409 required. The board has a USB port labeled "BIOS Flashback". The system won’t POST with the 5600 installed. How can you update the firmware?
options: Install Windows on another drive and run the vendor’s update utility.
Use the board’s BIOS Flashback feature with a formatted USB stick and the renamed BIOS file.
You cannot update; return the CPU or board.
Enter EZ‑Flash from BIOS Setup and update from USB.
concept_mcqs.explanation: BIOS Flashback updates firmware without a supported CPU or DRAM by using a dedicated microcontroller and USB port.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C: Both require a working POST/OS, which you don’t have. D: Flashback is designed for exactly this situation.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After enabling XMP, the system won’t POST. Manual excerpt:
```text
CLRTC (CMOS) Header: Short pins 1-2 for 10 seconds with system powered off to clear RTC RAM.
Also available: Rear-panel CLR_CMOS button.
```
What is the least‑risk immediate recovery step?
options: Short the CLRTC header with power removed to clear CMOS, then retry with defaults.
Remove the CPU to reset memory training data.
Increase DRAM voltage blindly to force POST.
Reflash BIOS to the latest version using EZ‑Flash.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Clearing CMOS is the standard, low‑risk recovery for failed overclock/XMP settings. It restores safe defaults without modifying firmware.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Reflashing is unnecessary and riskier than clearing CMOS. C: Removing the CPU is unrelated and adds risk. D: Blind voltage increases can damage components and don’t solve a failed POST caused by overly aggressive timings.

scenario_questions.scenario:
A client selected parts for a compact build:
```text
Case: mATX tower, GPU max length 300 mm, CPU cooler max height 158 mm
Motherboard: mATX B550, BIOS shipped v1004, Flashback supported
CPU: Ryzen 7 5800X (requires BIOS v2402+)
GPU: RTX 4070 Ti, length 320 mm, 2.5-slot
Cooler: Air tower 165 mm height
PSU: 650 W, 1x 4+4 EPS, 2x 6+2 PCIe
Drives: 1x NVMe, 2x SATA HDD (hot-swap bays in case front)
```
The client wants a same-day build that boots to BIOS and passes memory diagnostics (no OS install).
scenario_questions.task: Identify all blocking incompatibilities or risks that prevent a same-day successful BIOS boot and diagnostic run, and propose specific remedies for each. Prioritize actions and justify them against the artefacts provided.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Blocking issues: (1) GPU length 320 mm exceeds case 300 mm clearance. Remedy: choose a larger case or a shorter GPU; same-day path is to swap the case to one with ≥330 mm GPU clearance. (2) CPU cooler height 165 mm exceeds case 158 mm. Remedy: choose a cooler ≤158 mm or a 240 mm AIO that fits the case. (3) BIOS version v1004 cannot POST a 5800X; even if the board powers, it won’t train memory. Remedy: perform BIOS Flashback to v2402+ before CPU/RAM install or with only ATX/EPS power connected and a USB stick. Risks to check: (4) Ensure PSU has two 6+2 PCIe for GPU (it does) and one 8‑pin EPS (4+4) for CPU (meets required ATX_12V_8PIN; optional 4‑pin not required). (5) Front hot‑swap bays require SATA power and enabling Hot Plug per-port in BIOS later; not blocking for BIOS boot. Prioritization: swap case or GPU and cooler selection first (physical fit), then BIOS Flashback, then full assembly and diagnostics (MemTest86 one pass). Justifications reference the case clearance specs and vendor CPU support list.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies GPU length vs case clearance as a hard conflict
Correctly identifies cooler height vs case limit as a hard conflict
Correctly identifies BIOS version dependency and prescribes Flashback before POST
Prioritizes fixes logically (fitment first, firmware second) with justification tied to artefacts

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your training lab’s ESD workstation logs show:
```text
Mat Rs: 8.2 x 10^7 Ω (PASS)
Mat Rtg: OPEN (FAIL) via banana lead to CPC
Wrist strap test: PASS at 0.95 MΩ (operator + strap + cord)
RH: 23% (winter HVAC)
Ionizer: Available but OFF
Visual: Ground cord ring terminal corroded; snap fastener loose
```
Two more benches in the room test fine.
scenario_questions.task: Design a concrete, ordered remediation plan to bring this station into compliance today, with verification steps and acceptance thresholds for each fix. Explain why each step is necessary given the readings.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Plan: (1) Replace the mat ground cord (corroded) and reterminate to a verified common point ground shared with the passing benches. Verify Rtg ≤ 1.0 x 10^9 Ω with a megohmmeter using 5 lb electrode at 10 V (if spec’ed), document reading. (2) Replace or repair the loose snap fastener to ensure a reliable bond; recheck Rs (should remain 10^6–10^9 Ω) and Rtg. (3) Label and test the wrist strap path through the new common point ground using a continuous monitor or loop tester; document PASS with 0.75–1.25 MΩ. (4) Optional environmental control: If Rtg still marginal at low RH, turn on ionizer and set RH target to ~40% using local humidifier; verify ions balance (±50 V decay test if available). Acceptance: Rtg PASS and stable over 5 minutes; strap PASS; mat Rs unchanged in range; all grounds tagged and logged with date. Justification: The failure was bonding (OPEN), not surface resistivity; replacing/bonding fixes the only out-of-spec parameter. Environmental steps are secondary risk controls if readings drift due to dry air.

rubric.criterion: Orders actions to address the bonding fault first (ground cord/snap/CPC) with correct verification method
Specifies quantitative acceptance thresholds (Rtg, Rs, strap loop) and how to measure them
Explains why humidity/ionization is secondary given the data
Documents final compliance checks and labeling/logging

scenario_questions.scenario:
First power-on of a new build:
```text
Board: B450 (no POST with Ryzen 5000 on old BIOS)
Stickered BIOS: v1103
CPU: Ryzen 5 5600X
RAM: 2x16 GB DDR4‑3600
GPU: GTX 1060 (known-good)
Symptoms: Fans spin, DRAM Q‑LED solid; tried single stick in A2, CMOS clear, and reseat. Same.
```
Tools: USB drive, access to vendor BIOS files, board supports BIOS Flashback.
scenario_questions.task: Propose the next three diagnostic actions in order that have the highest chance to achieve a clean POST to BIOS today. For each, justify why it’s next, how to execute, and what success/failure implies for the subsequent step.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
1) BIOS Flashback to the latest version that adds Ryzen 5000 support (e.g., v2409): Rationale—B450 requires updated AGESA for 5600X memory training; DRAM LED may reflect IMC microcode mismatch. Execute with only ATX/EPS power, no CPU/RAM/GPU if supported; FAT32 USB with correct filename per vendor. Success: Board will then train memory; proceed to step 2. Failure: Rule out media/procedure; if persistently failing, suspect board.
2) After successful flash, install one DIMM in A2 at JEDEC 2133; disable XMP. Rationale—minimize training complexity. Success: POST to BIOS; then add second DIMM. Failure: Proceed to step 3.
3) Swap DIMM and slot to rule bad stick/slot; inspect CPU socket/pins (for AM4, bent pins on CPU) and standoffs causing shorts. Rationale—if firmware is current, remaining causes are hardware faults or shorts. Outcome directs RMA or board replacement.

rubric.criterion: Selects BIOS Flashback first with correct reasoning and execution details
Reduces memory config post‑flash to JEDEC single‑DIMM and explains why
Defines contingency checks (DIMM/slot swap, socket/standoff inspection) and next actions based on outcomes

scenario_questions.scenario:
You’re configuring firmware for a system with:
```text
Drives: NVMe M.2 (OS), SATA0/1 HDDs in hot‑swap bays
Current BIOS: CSM Enabled, SATA Mode RAID, Hot Plug Disabled, Secure Boot Disabled
Boot menu shows: UEFI USB, SATA0 HDD; NVMe present under NVMe Info
Goal: UEFI‑only boot from NVMe, SATA drives visible for data with hot‑plug working in OS later.
```
No OS install is performed today; you must still be able to boot to BIOS and validate detection.
scenario_questions.task: Specify the exact firmware changes to achieve the goal and the verification you will perform in BIOS to confirm success. Justify each setting change based on the hardware and desired behavior.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Changes: (1) Disable CSM (set UEFI Only). Justification—exposes NVMe boot paths; required for UEFI boot. (2) Set SATA Mode to AHCI (not RAID) since no array is planned; AHCI supports NCQ/hot‑plug better. (3) Enable Hot Plug on SATA0 and SATA1 ports only (matching the bay wiring). (4) Optionally enable Secure Boot after OS install; leave Disabled for now if using generic tools. Verification: After save/reboot, Boot Option Priorities should list the NVMe drive (or its UEFI entry) and not list Legacy options; NVMe Info should still show the device; SATA Configuration should show both HDDs with Hot Plug = Enabled; Hot Plug state visible in BIOS or via port info. Justification ties each setting to UEFI NVMe boot enumeration and correct SATA behavior for hot‑swap.

rubric.criterion: Disables CSM and justifies it for NVMe UEFI boot enumeration
Switches SATA controller to AHCI with correct reasoning
Enables Hot Plug on correct SATA ports and explains verification
Outlines BIOS‑level verification steps mapping to the goals

practical_tasks.title: Component identification and compatibility dossier
practical_tasks.brief: Identify and justify compatibility of core PC components before assembly. Work from real hardware on your bench. For each item, capture a clear photo and document the exact identifier, connector/form‑factor, and how it mates with the target motherboard/case/PSU. Cross‑reference with vendor manuals.
practical_tasks.deliverable:
One zipped folder containing: (a) a PDF or spreadsheet named components.csv or components.pdf with at least 20 rows (see required columns below); (b) a subfolder photos/ with one annotated photo per item, filename matching the Item_ID; (c) citation snippets (PDF pages or screenshots) from manuals/datasheets supporting each mapping.
Required columns: Item_ID, Component_Name, Exact_Model, Form_Factor/Slot (e.g., ATX24, EPS12V 8‑pin, M.2 2280, PCIe x16), Keying/Notch, Power_Req (if any), Target_Interface (board header/slot/port), Compatibility_Reason (1–2 sentences) with manual/datasheet page reference.
acceptance_criteria: At least 20 distinct components identified, including: motherboard power headers (ATX_24, EPS_8), CPU cooler mount, 1x PCIe GPU, 2x memory DIMMs, 1x storage (NVMe or SATA), front‑panel headers (PWR_SW, PLED, HDD_LED), at least 2 fan headers, and one case I/O connector.
Every row has a matching, legible annotated photo highlighting the connector/feature.
Every row cites a specific manual/datasheet page or figure that confirms form factor and pinout; citations included as images/PDF snippets.
Zero mismatches between documented interface and the photographed hardware (pin count/keying must match).
Submission opens cleanly; filenames consistent with Item_ID; no broken links.

rubric.criterion: Accuracy of identification (connector names, form factors, keying) across 20+ items
Compatibility justifications referencing the correct manual/datasheet sections
Quality and clarity of annotated photos linked to each row
Organization and completeness (all required columns present; filenames consistent)

practical_tasks.title: Assemble, configure firmware, and run pre‑OS diagnostics
practical_tasks.brief: Assemble a PC that reliably POSTs to BIOS/UEFI and completes memory/storage diagnostics without an OS. Configure cooling and firmware appropriately.
practical_tasks.deliverable: One zipped folder containing: (a) 6–10 build‑stage photos (CPU install, cooler mount, 24‑pin/EPS connected, GPU powered, front‑panel headers close‑up, cable management); (b) BIOS screenshots: Main (CPU/RAM detected), Hardware Monitor (temps/fan RPMs), Boot options (NVMe/SATA listed), BIOS version page; (c) MemTest86 or vendor UEFI memory test report showing at least 1 full pass with 0 errors; (d) Storage detection screenshot (BIOS NVMe Information or SATA Port list with drives); (e) a short text log (build_log.txt) listing any issues encountered and how you resolved them.
acceptance_criteria: System powers on and enters BIOS/UEFI without errors; screenshots show correct CPU model and total memory capacity in dual‑channel mode (if applicable).
Cooling configuration validated: BIOS Hardware Monitor shows CPU temperature ≤ 85°C sustained during a 5‑minute fan test; at least one CPU‑cooling device reports non‑zero RPM.
Boot configuration: CSM disabled or UEFI‑only noted if NVMe boot is desired; Boot menu shows the NVMe device (if installed).
Memory diagnostics: MemTest86 (or board UEFI test) completes 1+ full pass with 0 errors; attach the HTML/text report or photo evidence of PASS.
Storage: BIOS shows all connected drives; for SATA, ports are correctly enumerated; for NVMe, device details visible.
Firmware: BIOS version screenshot present; if CPU required a minimum version, note how you updated (e.g., Flashback) in build_log.txt.
ESD practice noted briefly in build_log.txt (strap/mat usage).

rubric.criterion: Functional assembly evidenced by BIOS detection (CPU, RAM in dual‑channel, drives) and photos
Correct and safe firmware configuration (UEFI/CSM, fan control) with justification in log
Successful diagnostic artifacts (MemTest result; storage visibility)
Build quality and risk controls (proper power cabling, cooler seating, ESD practices) shown in photos/log

concept_mcqs.stem:
You boot Windows Setup on a desktop whose firmware is currently set to Legacy (CSM). The target SSD already contains data you must preserve. Windows Setup shows:

```text
Windows cannot be installed to this disk. The selected disk is of the GPT partition style.
```

From Shift+F10 you run `diskpart`:

```text
diskpart
list disk

  Disk ###  Status         Size     Free     Dyn  Gpt
  --------  -------------  -------  -------  ---  ---
  Disk 0    Online          476 GB      0 B         *
```

Without deleting or re-partitioning the disk, which change allows you to proceed with installation?
options: Disable Secure Boot, keep Legacy mode, and let Setup continue on the GPT disk.
Create a 16 MB MSR partition in the free space to satisfy GPT requirements and retry setup.
Switch the firmware to UEFI mode, then reboot the installer so it installs to the existing GPT disk.
Run `diskpart` and `convert mbr` to change the disk to MBR without touching data.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Legacy (BIOS/CSM) cannot boot from a GPT disk. Changing the firmware to UEFI matches the existing GPT layout and lets Setup proceed without wiping partitions.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: `convert mbr` destroys partitions; the question forbids data loss. C: The disk has no free space, and adding an MSR does not make BIOS boot GPT. D: Secure Boot is unrelated; BIOS cannot boot GPT regardless of Secure Boot state.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A UEFI Windows 10 system fails to boot. From WinRE you find the EFI System Partition (ESP) exists but has no drive letter. `bcdedit` cannot open the store. `bootrec /rebuildbcd` finds 0 installations. Volumes are:

```text
diskpart
list vol

  Volume ###  Ltr  Label        Fs     Type        Size     Status     Info
  ----------  ---  -----------  -----  ----------  -------  ---------  --------
  Volume 0     C                NTFS   Partition    222 GB  Healthy    
  Volume 1                      FAT32  Partition    100 MB  Healthy    Hidden  (EFI)
```

What is the most direct next step to make the system bootable again?
options: Assign a letter to the ESP and run `bcdboot C:\Windows /s S: /f UEFI` to repopulate the EFI files.
Mark Volume 0 as Active and reboot so firmware finds the loader.
Run `bootrec /fixmbr` and `bootrec /fixboot` to repair the boot sector on Disk 0.
Run Startup Repair repeatedly until it discovers Windows and rebuilds the BCD automatically.
concept_mcqs.explanation: On UEFI/GPT systems you must place the boot files on the ESP. Mounting the ESP and using `bcdboot` repopulates the EFI files and BCD for the detected Windows installation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: `fixmbr`/`fixboot` apply to BIOS/MBR; UEFI uses the ESP, not the MBR boot code. B: GPT disks do not use an Active flag for UEFI boot. D: Startup Repair can loop and does not mount/write the ESP if it cannot locate Windows; `bcdboot` is the deterministic fix here.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Feature updates fail with 0x800f081f. From an elevated prompt you run:

```powershell
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

Error: 0x800f081f
The source files could not be found.
```

You have a Windows 10 ISO mounted as D: that matches the installed edition. Which command is most likely to succeed next?
options:
```powershell
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth /Source:WIM:D:\sources\install.wim:6 /LimitAccess
```

```powershell
DISM /Image:D:\ /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
```

```powershell
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup /ResetBase
```

```powershell
sfc /scannow
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: When DISM cannot find source files online, pointing it at a matching image WIM index and using `/LimitAccess` lets it get components locally. The other commands do not provide the missing source or target the correct image.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: SFC checks file integrity but does not repair the component store without sources. C: Targets the ISO volume, not the offline Windows directory. D: Component cleanup may reduce size but will not repair missing components without a source.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After installing a new graphics driver, the system BSODs at boot. In Safe Mode, Device Manager shows the device with the new driver. The Roll Back button is greyed out. You list third‑party drivers:

```powershell
pnputil /enum-drivers | findstr /i "oem.*display"

oem42.inf
    Driver package provider:  ContosoGPU
    Class:                    Display adapters
    Driver date and version:  03/20/2026  31.0.15.1234
    Signer name:              Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher
```

What is the most surgical way to recover boot without restoring the whole system?
options: Use System Restore to roll the OS back to a previous checkpoint.

```powershell
pnputil /delete-driver oem42.inf /uninstall /force
```

```powershell
sfc /scannow
```
Disable the GPU in BIOS to force the iGPU to take over.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Removing the specific problematic driver package with `pnputil` in Safe Mode rolls the device back to the previous working driver without affecting unrelated components.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: SFC does not manage third‑party driver package rollback. C: Works only if a suitable restore point exists and reverts unrelated changes. D: Many systems cannot disable the dGPU, and it avoids the root cause rather than fixing the driver state.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Reset this PC fails because Windows RE is disabled. On the affected machine:

```powershell
reagentc /info

Windows RE status: Disabled
Windows RE location: 
```

A previous upgrade left behind:

```text
C:\Windows.old\Windows\System32\Recovery\Winre.wim
```

What sequence correctly restores WinRE?
options:
```powershell
reagentc /setreimage /path C:\Windows.old\Windows\System32\Recovery
reagentc /enable
```

```powershell
copy C:\Windows.old\Windows\System32\Recovery\Winre.wim C:\Windows\WinSxS\
reagentc /enable
```

```powershell
bcdboot C:\Windows /s C:
```

```powershell
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: Point `reagentc` at a valid `Winre.wim` path and enable it. Using the existing image in Windows.old is acceptable, after which WinRE becomes available for Reset/Recovery.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Copying into WinSxS does not register WinRE. C: `bcdboot` rebuilds boot files, not WinRE configuration. D: Component cleanup doesn’t enable or register WinRE.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A workstation intermittently freezes. Event Viewer shows during freezes:

```text
Log: System
Source: iaStorAC
Event ID: 129
Message: Reset to device, \Device\RaidPort0, was issued.
```

The system has a single NVMe SSD, no RAID configured, and uses Intel RST driver for storage. What action is most likely to eliminate the freezes with minimal disruption?
options: Run `chkdsk /r` on the system volume to repair bad sectors.
Replace the Intel RST storage driver with the Microsoft Standard NVM Express Controller driver.
Disable write caching on the SSD to reduce queue depth.
Switch SATA mode in firmware to AHCI without any OS prep.
concept_mcqs.explanation: On non‑RAID NVMe systems, using the generic Microsoft NVMe driver instead of Intel RST often resolves Event 129 timeouts. It is a targeted, low‑risk change.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Disabling write caching hurts performance and does not address controller timeouts. C: Event 129s are typically driver/controller timeouts, not filesystem corruption; a surface scan won’t fix it. D: Changing storage mode blindly can make Windows unbootable without registry prep.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A desktop is very slow and the user reports occasional clicking sounds. You capture SMART and disk status:

```powershell
wmic diskdrive get Model,Status

Model                     Status
WDC WD10EZEX-00BN5A0      Pred Fail
```

What should you do first to minimize risk of data loss?
options: Disable Windows Search indexing to reduce I/O pressure and monitor.
Defragment the disk to improve performance, then back up.
Run `chkdsk /r` to repair sectors before attempting backup.
Back up or image the disk immediately and schedule a replacement drive.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A SMART "Pred Fail" indicates impending hardware failure. Prioritize getting a full backup or image and replace the drive; further stress can accelerate failure.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: `chkdsk /r` increases stress and may worsen failure before data is secured. C: Defragmenting adds heavy I/O to a failing disk. D: Indexing changes won’t change imminent failure risk; backup takes priority.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A USB printer intermittently disconnects when plugged into an unpowered hub. Device Manager shows:

```text
Unknown USB Device (Device Descriptor Request Failed)  Code 43
```

Which next step is the best low‑effort diagnostic that also often resolves the fault?
options: Disable USB selective suspend globally via Power Options.
Connect the printer directly to a motherboard USB 2.0 port with the OEM cable and external power, then install the vendor driver.
Reset the PC and perform an in‑place upgrade repair of Windows.
Uninstall all USB Root Hub devices from Device Manager and reboot to re‑enumerate.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Unpowered hubs can starve devices; moving to a direct, known‑good USB 2.0 port with proper power removes power and hub variables and is a standard diagnostic. Install the vendor driver afterwards.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Selective suspend can cause issues but is less likely than power insufficiency here. C: Blanket removal is disruptive and rarely necessary. D: Reinstalling Windows is excessive for a likely power/driver issue.

concept_mcqs.stem: You maintain a Windows image offline and need Realtek NIC support on deployment. The mounted image is at `C:\mount`. The signed driver `Netrtx64.inf` is in `D:\Drivers\Realtek\`. Which command correctly injects the driver into the offline image?
options:
```powershell
pnputil /add-driver D:\Drivers\Realtek\Netrtx64.inf /install
```

```powershell
DISM /Image:C:\ /Add-Driver /Driver:D:\Drivers\Realtek\ /Recurse
```

```powershell
DISM /Online /Add-Driver /Driver:D:\Drivers\Realtek /Recurse
```

```powershell
DISM /Image:C:\mount /Add-Driver /Driver:D:\Drivers\Realtek\Netrtx64.inf
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: To service an offline image, target the mount point with `/Image:` and point DISM at the specific signed `.inf` (or use `/Recurse` on the folder).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Targets the running OS (`/Online`), not the offline image. C: `pnputil` manages drivers on the running OS, not an offline WIM. D: Targets the host drive root, not the mounted image path.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A PC hangs for 30 seconds at boot whenever a non‑bootable USB flash drive is left plugged in. Current boot order (UEFI):

```text
1. USB Storage Device
2. SATA0: WDC WD5000...
3. Windows Boot Manager
4. Network Boot (PXE)
```

You want the machine to boot normally with USB devices attached. What change achieves this with least side effects?
options: Enable Legacy (CSM) mode so BIOS skips non‑bootable USB devices.
Set the internal disk as Active so firmware ignores USB devices.
Move Windows Boot Manager to the top of the boot order or disable USB Storage boot.
Format the USB drive as NTFS so the firmware can read it faster.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Ensure the firmware tries the internal OS loader first or simply disables USB storage boot. Then attached non‑bootable USB devices will not delay startup.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Enabling CSM changes boot mode and can break UEFI installs. C: The Active flag is irrelevant for UEFI and does not control device priority. D: Filesystem on the USB doesn’t fix boot priority delays.

scenario_questions.scenario:
A small office desktop with Windows 10 Pro and a single NVMe SSD started looping into “Automatic Repair couldn’t repair your PC” right after a vendor “Intel Rapid Storage Technology” update. The system has no RAID and uses UEFI/GPT. From WinRE Command Prompt:

```text
bcdedit -> The boot configuration data store could not be opened.
diskpart -> ESP present as 100 MB FAT32, no letter
SrtTrail.txt -> Boot critical driver: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\iaStorAC.sys is corrupt
```
scenario_questions.task: Propose a recovery plan that restores boot with minimal disruption. Specify the exact sequence of actions and tools/commands you would use, and why each is chosen. Include how you will verify success and prevent recurrence.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
A strong answer proposes: 1) Offline driver rollback for the storage stack, 2) ensure boot files are healthy, 3) verification and prevention.

Sequence example: Mount ESP and repopulate boot files to eliminate bootloader issues: `diskpart` assign letter S: to the ESP; `bcdboot C:\Windows /s S: /f UEFI`. Then remove the faulty RST driver offline from Safe Mode or WinRE: `pnputil /delete-driver oemXX.inf /uninstall /force` targeting `iaStorAC` package, or use `dism /image:C:\ /get-drivers` to identify and `/remove-driver` to remove. Alternatively, switch the storage controller to the Microsoft Standard NVM Express Controller by disabling/renaming `iaStorAC.sys` (as last resort). Reboot. Verify by clean boot to desktop, Event Viewer free of new 129/iaStorAC errors, and Device Manager showing the Microsoft NVMe driver. Prevent recurrence by: pinning a known‑good storage driver, blocking that specific update via policy (wushowhide or GPO for device installation restrictions), and documenting the OEM‑recommended driver for non‑RAID systems.

rubric.criterion: Identifies storage driver as root cause and chooses rollback/replacement over OS reinstall
Uses correct UEFI repair step with bcdboot and ESP mounting rather than BIOS/MBR fixes
Provides concrete offline servicing commands (pnputil or DISM) and safe booting path
Verification (Event Viewer, Device Manager driver state) and a realistic prevention plan

scenario_questions.scenario: You must install Windows 11 on a UEFI‑only laptop. The first USB you created with default Rufus settings will not boot; the firmware lists it but skips straight to the existing OS. The USB was prepared as MBR/NTFS. Secure Boot is enabled. You have the Windows 11 ISO and can recreate media.
scenario_questions.task: Decide how to recreate the installation media and what firmware settings (if any) to change. Justify your choices so the stick boots reliably without compromising security.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Explain that the laptop expects UEFI‑bootable, FAT32 media. Recreate the USB as GPT partitioned with a single FAT32 partition and copy the ISO contents, or use a tool that creates UEFI‑compatible media (Rufus: Partition scheme GPT, Target system UEFI (no CSM), File system FAT32). If `install.wim` exceeds 4 GB, use a tool that splits it automatically or split manually; do not switch to NTFS because many UEFI implementations cannot boot NTFS with Secure Boot on. Keep Secure Boot enabled; no need to enable CSM/Legacy. Optionally disable Fast Boot temporarily if firmware hides USB prompts. Outcome: USB now boots in UEFI with Secure Boot intact.

rubric.criterion: Selects GPT + FAT32 media format compatible with UEFI and Secure Boot
Explains why NTFS/MBR media failed in UEFI‑only + Secure Boot context
Addresses >4 GB WIM handling without disabling Secure Boot
Justifies avoiding CSM/Legacy and unnecessary security downgrades

scenario_questions.scenario: After a standard user rename, the user can no longer sign in. Message: “The User Profile Service failed the sign‑in.” The filesystem still has `C:\Users\oldname` with data. In `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList`, one SID’s `ProfileImagePath` points to `C:\Users\oldname`, and a duplicate SID with `.bak` exists.
scenario_questions.task: Describe how you will safely restore a working profile without data loss. Include exact registry and filesystem changes, and how you will validate the fix.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Create a full backup or restore point first. Sign in as an admin. In `ProfileList`, identify the SID with `.bak`. If the non‑`.bak` subkey is broken (e.g., wrong path), swap keys per Microsoft guidance: rename the non‑`.bak` key to `.bad`, remove `.bak` from the other to make it active, and set its `State` to 0 and `RefCount` to 0. Ensure `ProfileImagePath` points to the correct folder (either keep `C:\Users\oldname` or rename the folder and update the path consistently). Fix NTFS permissions on the profile folder to the SID. Reboot and test login. Validate by successful sign‑in, correct profile path in `whoami /user` SID mapping, and intact user data. Avoid creating a new profile unless mapping is impossible; that can orphan data.

rubric.criterion: Backs up and operates under an admin context with rollback plan
Correctly handles `.bak` vs non‑`.bak` SID keys and sets State/RefCount
Ensures `ProfileImagePath` and filesystem folder/permissions align
Validation steps after reboot (successful login, data intact)

scenario_questions.scenario: During large file copies to an external USB 3.0 HDD, a laptop freezes for seconds and the copy fails. On USB 2.0, it works. Logs show Kernel‑PnP Event 219 (Driver failed to load) for the USB 3.0 controller and multiple `usbstor` resets. The drive works on another PC with the same cable.
scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the most likely root cause chain and propose a test plan plus fixes in order of least to most invasive. Justify each step.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Likely causes: power delivery or controller/driver instability on this laptop’s USB 3.0 host. Start with least invasive: try a different USB 3.0 port on the laptop (separate root hub), then a powered USB 3.0 hub or the drive’s Y‑cable/external power to rule out power sag. Update the laptop’s chipset/USB 3.0 host controller driver from OEM and system firmware (UEFI). Check Power Options: disable “USB selective suspend” for testing only. If events persist, check Device Manager for power management on the hub/controller (uncheck allow the computer to turn off). Validate with sustained transfer test and Event Viewer free of 219/`usbstor` resets. If still failing, suspect the laptop’s USB 3.0 hardware; use USB 2.0 or a known‑good USB‑C dock with external power as a workaround; plan board repair if under warranty.

rubric.criterion: Identifies host controller/power delivery as primary suspects given symptoms
Proposes a clear, low‑to‑high invasiveness test sequence (ports, powered hub, drivers/firmware)
Includes specific OS settings to test (selective suspend, power management) with justification
Defines validation metrics (sustained copy, absence of errors in logs)

practical_tasks.title: Provision a clean, recoverable workstation
practical_tasks.brief: Install Windows on a bare‑metal or virtual PC, load required drivers, create users, apply updates, and configure recovery so the machine is supportable. Capture verifiable artefacts on the workstation to prove configuration without assessor guesswork.
acceptance_criteria: The workstation boots UEFI to Windows 10/11. Evidence on the workstation at C:\NTC030-S02\ contains: `systeminfo.txt` (shows BIOS mode UEFI), `diskpart-list.txt` (shows EFI, MSR, OS partitions), and a `winver.png` screenshot.
All devices have drivers installed (no yellow bangs). Evidence: `devmgmt.png` and `pnputil-list.txt` (`pnputil /enum-drivers`) saved to C:\NTC030-S02\.
Local accounts: one standard user and one administrator as per naming in your submission notes. Evidence: `net-localgroup.txt` outputs for `administrators` and `users`.
Windows Update fully applied at submission time. Evidence: `wmic qfe list brief /format:table` saved as `updates.txt` and `USOClient startscan` timestamp in `update-log.txt`.

Recovery is working: `reagentc /info` shows Windows RE Enabled; at least one Restore Point exists named NTC030-S02. Evidence: `reagentc-info.txt` and a `vssadmin list shadows` or `PowerShell Get-ComputerRestorePoint` output.

A tested, scriptable backup exists: either a full system image to a secondary disk/VM virtual disk using `wbAdmin start backup -backupTarget:<path> -include:C: -allCritical -quiet` (or vendor imaging tool). Evidence: the command output saved to `backup-log.txt` and the backup file listing `dir` of the target path.

rubric.criterion: UEFI/GPT installation and OS version validated by captured artefacts
Driver state clean and evidenced (Device Manager and pnputil outputs)
Users created with correct roles and evidence of group memberships
Updates applied with verifiable hotfix/QFE listing
Recovery configured (WinRE enabled, restore point present) with proof
Backup/image created and evidenced by logs and file listings

practical_tasks.title: Produce a fault‑resolution log for two system issues
practical_tasks.brief: Investigate and resolve two faults on a Windows workstation: one affecting boot/startup and one affecting performance, storage, or a peripheral. Capture a technician‑grade log that demonstrates disciplined troubleshooting, commands used, and hard evidence of resolution.
acceptance_criteria: One boot/startup fault documented end‑to‑end (e.g., BCD/EFI issue, startup driver failure).
One non‑boot fault documented end‑to‑end (performance spike, storage SMART warning, or peripheral malfunction).

Each case includes: symptoms, environment, initial hypotheses, tests performed, commands and outputs (e.g., `bcdboot`, `DISM`, `sfc`, `eventvwr` exports, `wmic` SMART, `resmon` screenshots), and final resolution with root cause.
Each case includes prevention/next steps and verification evidence (before/after logs or screenshots).
The log is provided as a single PDF or markdown file placed at C:\NTC030-S02\fault-log.(pdf|md), with all referenced artefacts present under C:\NTC030-S02\evidence\ and clearly cross‑referenced.

rubric.criterion: Clear problem statements and environment context for both cases
Systematic hypotheses and test plan demonstrating troubleshooting thinking
Accurate use of appropriate tools/commands with captured evidence
Sound root cause analysis and justified resolution steps
Verification and preventive recommendations for each case

concept_mcqs.stem:
You are handed these outputs after a failed ping from PC1 to its default gateway.

```text
PC1 ipconfig
-------------------------
IPv4 Address . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.50
Subnet Mask  . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.128
Default Gateway . . . . . . . .  : 192.168.10.129

Router R1 (LAN interface)
-------------------------
GigabitEthernet0/0 IP address: 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.128

PC1> ping 192.168.10.1
Request timed out.
```
What explains the failure?
options: PC1’s default gateway is not in PC1’s local subnet; ARP for 192.168.10.129 never succeeds so PC1 has no route off-net.
PC1 should use a /24 mask so it can ARP for 192.168.10.1; with /25 ARP is blocked.
PC1’s IP and gateway are in the same /25, but the router is blocking ICMP. The network is otherwise fine.
The router’s mask is too small; it should be 255.255.255.0 to reach 192.168.10.50 directly.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With a /25 mask, 192.168.10.0–127 is one subnet and 128–255 is another. PC1 (192.168.10.50/25) is in 192.168.10.0/25, but its configured gateway 192.168.10.129 is in 192.168.10.128/25, so PC1 cannot ARP for the gateway. The ping to 192.168.10.1 also fails because PC1 believes 192.168.10.1 is local but the router interface actually has that IP; however the immediate failure here is the unusable gateway. Fix the gateway to 192.168.10.1 for this /25.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: A /24 would place all in one subnet, but the router’s /25 is consistent with PC1’s mask; the core issue is the gateway address, not mask size. C: ARP is not “blocked” by a /25; 192.168.10.1 is within PC1’s /25 and could be ARPed; the incorrect gateway is the blocker for off-net traffic. D: If IP/gateway were in the same /25 and ICMP blocked, other off-net traffic would still work; here the default gateway is unreachable by design.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A frame arrives on an unmanaged switch with the following MAC address table. The incoming frame arrives on port Fa0/4 with source MAC DD-DD-DD-DD-DD-DD and destination MAC BB-BB-BB-BB-BB-BB.

```text
Switch MAC Table
---------------------------
MAC                   Port
AA-AA-AA-AA-AA-AA     Fa0/1
BB-BB-BB-BB-BB-BB     Fa0/2
CC-CC-CC-CC-CC-CC     Fa0/3
<no entry>            Fa0/4
```
What happens next?
options: Drops the frame because destination is unicast and unknown on Fa0/4.
Learns DD on Fa0/4; floods to all ports except Fa0/4 because destination is broadcast-unknown.
Floods the frame out Fa0/1, Fa0/2, and Fa0/3 because DD is unknown.
Learns DD on Fa0/4; forwards the frame only out Fa0/2.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Switches learn the source MAC on ingress. DD is learned on Fa0/4. Because the destination BB is a known unicast on Fa0/2, the frame is forwarded only out Fa0/2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Unknown destination unicast would be flooded, but the destination BB is known. C: Broadcast frames are flooded, but this destination is a known unicast. D: Switches do not drop unknown unicasts by default; they flood them. Here it’s not unknown anyway.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A 1 Gbps uplink between two switches is unstable. Your cable tester shows:

```text
Cable Certifier Report (Link A1)
--------------------------------
Media: UTP Cat6
Pair Lengths (m): 1-2: 118, 3-6: 119, 4-5: 118, 7-8: 119
Wiremap: PASS (TIA-568B)
NEXT: Marginal
Result: 1000BASE-T FAIL, 100BASE-TX PASS
```
What most directly explains the 1 Gbps instability?
options: Duplex mismatch; 1000BASE-T requires full duplex and the switches are set to half duplex.
Wrong pinout at one end (568A/568B mismatch) creating a crossover that 1 Gbps cannot negotiate over.
Horizontal copper run exceeds the 100 m channel limit; attenuation and NEXT prevent 1000BASE-T but 100BASE-TX can limp by.
EMI from fluorescent lighting; 1000BASE-T is more EMI-prone than 100BASE-TX.
concept_mcqs.explanation: 1000BASE-T requires the full channel to be within spec up to 100 m. The ~118–119 m run exceeds the maximum channel length, leading to attenuation/NEXT issues that break 1 G but sometimes allow 100 Mb to pass.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: EMI can hurt links, but the report pinpoints marginal NEXT and overlength; EMI isn’t evidenced. C: A vs B determines crossover, which modern PHYs (especially 1G with auto MDI-X) handle; the wiremap shows PASS with consistent 568B. D: Duplex isn’t the cause of physical layer rate downshift/failure reported by the certifier.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You scan 2.4 GHz in an office before placing one AP.

```text
2.4 GHz Scan (center-channel RSSI)
----------------------------------
Ch 1: SSID NET-1  RSSI -40 dBm
Ch 6: SSID NET-2  RSSI -65 dBm
Ch11: SSID NET-3  RSSI -70 dBm
Your AP location RSSI to clients: ~ -55 dBm (estimated)
```
To minimize contention for your clients at this location, which channel should you set?
options: Channel 1
Auto channel selection with 40 MHz width on channels 6+10
Channel 6
Channel 11
concept_mcqs.explanation: With a very strong neighbor on channel 1 (-40), channel 11 is the cleanest of the three non-overlapping options. Channel 6 is acceptable but has a stronger neighbor than 11.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Viable, but 11 has slightly weaker observed neighbor interference than 6, making 11 better here. C: Channel 1 has a very strong interferer at -40 dBm, likely causing contention and CCA backoffs. D: 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz overlaps multiple channels and worsens interference; auto may still land badly in this congested band.

concept_mcqs.stem: You must carve 172.16.8.0/24 into two LANs: one for up to 90 hosts and one for up to 28 hosts, using a router with two LAN interfaces. Which plan both fits and avoids overlap?
concept_mcqs.explanation: /25 gives 126 hosts (fits 90). A /27 gives 30 hosts (fits 28). 172.16.8.0/25 uses .0–.127 and 172.16.8.128/27 uses .128–.159; they do not overlap.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: /26 holds only 62 hosts, not enough for 90. C: /64/25 (172.16.8.64–.191) overlaps 172.16.8.0/27 unless carefully ordered; as written, they conflict. D: The /26 for 28 hosts is over-allocated and overlaps the preceding /25 (.64–.127).

concept_mcqs.stem:
Users report poor throughput on a single wired host. You check link stats:

```text
Switch Gi0/1: 100 Mb/s, Half Duplex, CRC errors rising, Late collisions present
Host NIC:     100 Mb/s, Full Duplex (manually configured)
```
What change most directly resolves this?
options: Force the switch to 100 Mb/s full duplex; leave the NIC as is.
Set both sides to auto-negotiate speed/duplex, or manually match them to 100 Mb/s full duplex.
Increase switch port speed to 1 Gb/s; duplex then won’t matter.
Disable flow control; collisions stop because NIC buffers frames.
concept_mcqs.explanation: This is a duplex mismatch (switch half, NIC full), causing CRC errors and late collisions. Duplex must match. Best practice is to set both to auto or both to the same fixed setting.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Forcing only the switch might fix it, but the correct action is to ensure both ends are aligned; recommending single-sided change is brittle. C: Speed/duplex still must match at 1 Gb; and 1G requires full duplex but both ends must negotiate. D: Flow control doesn’t resolve duplex mismatches or physical collisions on half-duplex links.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A cable passes a basic continuity test but a certifier reports a split pair on 3–6. The host links up to the switch but file copies crawl and errors increment.

```text
Wiremap: PASS
Pairing: FAIL (Split Pair 3-6)
100BASE-TX: MARGINAL   1000BASE-T: FAIL
Switch Port: CRC errors increasing under load
```
What symptom is most consistent with this cabling fault?
options: Link fails to come up at any speed because continuity must fail if pairs are split.
Only broadcasts are affected; unicasts pass because they use fewer pairs.
Link negotiates at 100 Mb/s with frequent CRC errors and retransmissions under load.
Link comes up at 1 Gb/s but pings are dropped only at night due to temperature.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Split pairs can pass simple continuity but fail NEXT, leading to high error rates. 1G will fail entirely; 100 Mb may come up but perform poorly with CRC errors and retransmissions.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Split pairs can pass continuity; that’s the trap. C: Temperature sensitivity is not the primary failure mode here; the cert shows a deterministic NEXT issue. D: Ethernet doesn’t treat broadcasts differently at the physical layer; errors would affect all traffic.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Observe a ping before and after an ARP cache clear.

```text
C:\> arp -d *
C:\> ping 10.0.1.1
Reply from 10.0.1.1: bytes=32 time=124ms TTL=63
Reply from 10.0.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=63
Reply from 10.0.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=63
Reply from 10.0.1.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=63

C:\> arp -a
Interface: 10.0.1.50 --- 0x7
  Internet Address      Physical Address      Type
  10.0.1.1              00-11-22-33-44-55     dynamic
```
What explains the first high-latency reply?
options: The first echo waited for ARP resolution before the ICMP echo left; subsequent pings used the cached MAC.
ICMP is rate-limited on Windows for the first packet only; later ones are prioritized.
TTL on the first reply was decremented multiple times; later ones were not.
The switch flooded the first ping as an unknown broadcast; later ones were unicasts.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Clearing the ARP cache forces the host to ARP for the gateway or target. The first ICMP echo is delayed until the ARP completes; subsequent pings use the cached mapping and are fast.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Windows does not rate-limit just the first ICMP. C: TTL does not affect latency like this; it decrements on each hop regardless. D: Unknown unicast flooding occurs on switches but does not cause consistent first-packet latency tied to ARP state.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Two /26 subnets exist on the same access switch, terminated by a router with two LAN interfaces:

```text
LAN A: 192.168.1.0/26    Router LAN A IP: 192.168.1.1
LAN B: 192.168.1.64/26   Router LAN B IP: 192.168.1.65
Host H (on LAN B): IP 192.168.1.70  Mask 255.255.255.192  GW 192.168.1.1

H> ping 8.8.8.8  -> Request timed out
H> ping 192.168.1.65 -> Success
```
Why does H fail to reach the internet?
options: H’s default gateway is on the wrong subnet; it must be 192.168.1.65 for LAN B.
LAN B mask should be /24 so the router can route to the internet.
H’s IP must be changed to 192.168.1.10 to match the gateway subnet.
Switch cannot carry two subnets without VLANs, so routing is impossible.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Host H lives in 192.168.1.64/26 and must use the router IP in that subnet (192.168.1.65) as its default gateway. Using 192.168.1.1 strands its off-net traffic.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: The /26 is fine; routing off-net depends on the correct gateway, not a /24. C: The host IP need not change; the gateway must. D: Two subnets can exist on the same physical switch if the router has two interfaces into that switch (or separate access ports). VLANs are not strictly required here.

concept_mcqs.stem: A single AP serves a meeting room with mixed 2.4/5 GHz clients. Current config is 2.4 GHz only, 20 MHz width, channel 6, TX power high. Throughput is inconsistent and neighboring scans show multiple -50 to -60 dBm APs on channels 1, 6, and 11. What change most likely stabilizes client throughput?
options: Bond 40 MHz on 2.4 GHz to double throughput.
Enable 5 GHz on a low-usage channel (e.g., 36) at moderate power; leave 2.4 GHz at 20 MHz.
Disable 2.4 GHz entirely; 5 GHz only will guarantee compatibility and stability.
Raise 2.4 GHz transmit power further to overcome neighbors.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Moving capable clients to 5 GHz reduces co-channel contention; moderate power limits cell size and CCI. Keeping 2.4 GHz at 20 MHz preserves legacy support without causing excessive overlap.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: 40 MHz on 2.4 causes heavy overlap and more contention, worsening stability. C: Raising power increases cell size and co-channel interference, likely making contention worse. D: Disabling 2.4 breaks legacy clients that cannot use 5 GHz; stability should not come at the expense of required compatibility.

scenario_questions.scenario:
You are given this partial small-office network plan. One router (R1) connects two access switches (SW-A for Staff, SW-B for IoT). Cabling between R1 and each switch is separate copper links. The address block available is 10.20.30.0/24.

```text
Requirements
-----------
Staff LAN: 80 wired hosts today, growth to 110
IoT LAN:   18 devices (printers, cameras), static IPs preferred
R1 has two FastEthernet LAN interfaces: FE0/0 -> SW-A, FE0/1 -> SW-B

Proposed config (by a junior)
-----------------------------
Staff LAN: 10.20.30.0/26, GW 10.20.30.1 on R1 FE0/0
IoT LAN:   10.20.30.64/27, GW 10.20.30.65 on R1 FE0/1
```
After cutover, some staff can’t get addresses within the planned range and a few cannot reach the internet intermittently. IoT works fine. DHCP for Staff is on a server in the Staff LAN, default gateway points to R1. No VLANs are in use.
scenario_questions.task: Identify the exact planning fault(s) in the junior’s proposal and produce a corrected subnet plan and gateway assignment that meets the requirements with minimal renumbering. Justify the mask choices and show usable host ranges for each LAN.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
The Staff /26 (10.20.30.0–.63) supports only 62 usable hosts, insufficient for 80–110. The IoT /27 (10.20.30.64–.95) is fine for 18 static devices (30 usable). Correct approach: allocate a /25 to Staff and a /27 (or /26) to IoT. For minimal renumbering within 10.20.30.0/24:
- Staff LAN: 10.20.30.0/25 (usable .1–.126), GW 10.20.30.1 on R1 FE0/0. Supports up to 126 hosts.
- IoT LAN: 10.20.30.128/27 (usable .129–.158), GW 10.20.30.129 on R1 FE0/1. If more headroom desired, use 10.20.30.128/26 (usable .129–.190).
Justification: /25 satisfies 110 target; /27 covers 18 IoT devices with room. Avoid overlap by placing IoT block in the upper half. Intermittent internet was due to Staff clients being assigned beyond .63 when DHCP scope was mis-sized relative to /26, causing some to be off-subnet or conflicting; with /25 the DHCP scope can be .50–.120 (example) within usable range.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies that /26 for Staff is undersized and quantifies host capacity vs requirement
Proposes a corrected mask for Staff that supports growth (e.g., /25) and assigns a correct gateway within that subnet
Allocates a non-overlapping subnet for IoT (e.g., /27 or /26 in upper range) with correct usable range and gateway
Provides a clear justification (why the chosen masks, avoiding overlap) and ties it to the observed intermittent failures (scope overrun/off-subnet)

scenario_questions.scenario: A rectangular single-floor office (40 m x 15 m) needs two APs to cover open-plan seating. A walkthrough scan shows heavy 2.4 GHz occupancy on channels 1 and 6 around -55 dBm from neighbors and a weaker -72 dBm on channel 11. The 5 GHz band shows light use on channels 36 and 44. The APs will be ceiling-mounted ~20 m apart along the long axis. Most client devices support 5 GHz, but a few handheld scanners are 2.4 GHz-only.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a channel and power plan for both APs that minimizes co-channel interference while keeping legacy devices working. State the exact 2.4 and 5 GHz channels and whether to use 20/40 MHz. Include TX power considerations and explain your trade-offs.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Use both bands. For 2.4 GHz, assign AP1 channel 11 and AP2 channel 1, both at 20 MHz, with reduced transmit power (e.g., medium/low so cells don’t overlap at strong RSSI). Avoid channel 6 due to strong neighbors. For 5 GHz, assign AP1 channel 36 and AP2 channel 44 (non-overlapping), at 20 MHz (or 40 MHz if survey confirms low occupancy), with moderate power so 5 GHz carries most load. This balances legacy 2.4-only scanners (served by small 2.4 cells) and encourages dual-band clients onto 5 GHz with minimal CCI.

rubric.criterion: Chooses appropriate non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels and justifies avoiding congested channels
Selects suitable 5 GHz channels with bandwidth choice and explains when 20 vs 40 MHz is acceptable
Addresses transmit power settings to manage cell size and reduce co-channel contention
Explains the trade-off to keep legacy 2.4 GHz clients working while offloading capable clients to 5 GHz

scenario_questions.scenario: You must link an MDF to an IDF 140 m away through an industrial area with motors and fluorescent lighting. The IDF will host a small access switch and two PoE APs. The MDF has the core switch and router. Budget is modest but downtime is costly.
scenario_questions.task: Recommend the physical media and connectivity approach end-to-end, including how to power the APs, and justify against distance, EMI, and PoE requirements. Specify connector types and any needed conversion equipment.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Use multimode fiber (OM3/OM4) between MDF and IDF for the 140 m uplink to avoid copper’s 100 m limit and EMI issues. Terminate with LC connectors and use SFP transceivers in both switches. In the IDF, deploy a PoE access switch powered locally (or non-PoE switch plus midspan PoE injector(s)) to feed the two APs over short copper runs. Rationale: Fiber immune to EMI and supports >1 Gbps over 140 m; copper would exceed spec and be noise-prone. PoE cannot traverse fiber, so PoE must originate in the IDF via a PoE switch or injectors.

rubric.criterion: Selects fiber for the 140 m interconnect and explains distance/EMI justification
Specifies appropriate fiber type (e.g., OM3/OM4) and LC/SFP details at both ends
Explains PoE delivery at the IDF (PoE switch or injectors) since PoE cannot run over fiber
Provides a coherent end-to-end plan (MDF to IDF to APs) that is practically actionable

scenario_questions.scenario:
A contractor submits this addressing for a training lab with two routed VLAN-less segments on separate router interfaces (router has FE0/0 and FE0/1 to the same access switch on different access ports). You are asked to validate the plan for 60 student PCs (wired) and 15 lab devices (printers/APs), with the given /24.

```text
Given block: 192.168.50.0/24
Proposed:
  Student LAN: 192.168.50.64/27, GW 192.168.50.65
  Devices LAN: 192.168.50.0/26,  GW 192.168.50.1
```
Spot any issues and provide a corrected plan that meets host counts and uses the /24 efficiently. Include gateway placements and usable ranges.
scenario_questions.task: Evaluate the proposal, point out any capacity/overlap issues, then produce a corrected subnetting plan with justifications and ranges for each LAN.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The Student LAN needs 60 hosts; /27 allows only 30. Devices need 15 hosts; /26 allows 62 and is oversized but workable. Correct plan: assign Students a /26 and Devices a /27 without overlap. For example: Devices LAN 192.168.50.0/27 (usable .1–.30, GW .1) and Students LAN 192.168.50.64/26 (usable .65–.126, GW .65). Both fit and are contiguous within the /24 with no overlap.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the student /27 capacity shortfall accurately
Produces two non-overlapping subnets that satisfy 60 and 15 hosts respectively
Places gateways correctly within each subnet and provides correct usable ranges
Provides brief justification for efficiency and non-overlap within the /24

practical_tasks.title: Design a small-office network diagram with addressing and media plan
practical_tasks.brief: Create a logical network diagram for a 25–40 user office using a single router, one core switch, one access switch, and one AP. Show subnets, IP addressing, default gateways, cable media choices, and Wi-Fi channel plan. Assume you have 192.168.20.0/24 available and want two subnets: users and devices. Include cable types (Cat6 vs fiber), port labels, and link speeds. Keep within Layer 2 basics (no VLANs).

Each LAN has a clearly labeled network ID and mask; default gateway IPs shown on the router interfaces and within correct ranges.
Cable/media annotations for each link (e.g., Cat6 1G copper, or fiber if run >100 m), with any >100 m runs correctly set to fiber.

rubric.criterion: Logical correctness of topology (router with two LANs to two distinct L2 domains; devices sensibly placed)
Accurate subnetting and addressing (correct masks, gateways inside ranges, no overlaps)
Media choices justified on the diagram (fiber where needed, copper within 100 m, link speeds labeled)
Clear Wi-Fi channel/band plan noted and reasonable given a simple two-AP or one-AP setup
Clarity and consistency between diagram and addressing table (labels, IPs, ranges)

practical_tasks.title: Build a connected two-subnet lab and prove end-to-end connectivity
practical_tasks.brief: Using a simulator (e.g., Cisco Packet Tracer, GNS3) or equivalent lab gear, build two separate IPv4 subnets linked by a router. Place at least two PCs in each subnet via access switches. Optionally add an AP bridged to one subnet and connect one wireless client. Statically configure IPv4 addresses and default gateways. Choose and place the correct cable types between devices. Verify intra-subnet and inter-subnet connectivity with pings and capture ARP tables showing learned MACs.

Router has one interface in each subnet with the correct mask, and all hosts use the correct default gateway for their subnet.
Evidence of successful ping within a subnet and across subnets (host in subnet A to host in subnet B).
