End-to-end connectivity proof (intra- and inter-subnet pings succeed)
Layer 2 evidence (MAC/ARP tables align with topology after traffic)
Appropriate cabling selections and link states up/green throughout
Optional AP and wireless client bridged correctly (if included) without breaking wired connectivity

concept_mcqs.stem:
A Layer-3 switch routes between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. PCs in VLAN 10 cannot obtain DHCP leases from a DHCP server in VLAN 20.

Configs:

```text
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Vlan20
 ip address 10.20.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Fa0/10
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast
!
! DHCP server: 10.20.20.10 (in VLAN 20)
```

A packet capture on the Vlan10 SVI shows DHCPDISCOVER frames, but no DHCPOFFER arrives. Without moving any cables, which single configuration change on the switch will allow the PC in VLAN 10 to get a lease from the server in VLAN 20?
options:
```text
interface Fa0/10
 ip dhcp snooping trust
```

```text
interface Fa0/10
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
```
Add a `default-router 10.10.10.1` option to the DHCP scope on the server.

```text
interface Vlan10
 ip helper-address 10.20.20.10
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: DHCP is broadcast on the client VLAN and will not cross VLAN boundaries unless relayed. Adding an IP helper on Vlan10 relays the broadcast to the unicast DHCP server in VLAN 20.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is tempting because trunks carry multiple VLANs, but the PC is an access host and making it a trunk is incorrect and insecure. C is about DHCP snooping trust, which governs who may send server responses, not relay between VLANs. D sets the default gateway handed to clients but does not address the lack of broadcast relay between VLANs.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A DNS zone file contains the following records:

```text
$ORIGIN corp.local.
@     IN SOA ns1.corp.local. admin.corp.local. (
          2026010101 3600 600 1209600 300 )
      IN NS  ns1.corp.local.
ns1   IN A   10.10.10.10
app   IN A   10.10.10.50
cdn   IN CNAME assets.external.com   ; note the missing trailing dot
```

A resolver queries `cdn.corp.local.`. Which FQDN will the CNAME actually point to because of the missing trailing dot?
options: ns1.corp.local.
assets.external.com.
assets.external.com.corp.local.
A CNAME loop will occur and the query will time out.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Without a trailing dot, the CNAME target is treated as relative to the current origin, becoming `assets.external.com.corp.local.`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is what many expect, but the missing dot prevents it from being absolute. C is unrelated to the CNAME target. D suggests a generic failure; there is no loop defined here, just a wrong FQDN.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Inter-VLAN routing via router-on-a-stick is configured as follows. Hosts in VLAN 30 cannot reach VLAN 40; pings from 10.30.0.10 to 10.40.0.10 fail.

```text
interface g0/0
 no ip address
!
interface g0/0.30
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface g0/0.40
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 10.40.0.1 255.255.255.0
```

Which single change fixes inter-VLAN connectivity?
options:
```text
interface g0/0.40
 encapsulation dot1Q 40
```
Add a static route on the router for 10.40.0.0/24 via 10.30.0.1.

```text
interface g0/0
 ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0
```

```text
interface g0/0.40
 encapsulation dot1Q 40 native
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: The subinterface for VLAN 40 is using the wrong VLAN tag (30). Correcting it to `encapsulation dot1Q 40` will allow frames from VLAN 40 to be processed on the right subinterface.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B would destroy the router-on-a-stick design by assigning an IP to the physical interface. C would make VLAN 40 native, mismatching the switch trunk unless coordinated and still not the intended design. D is unnecessary; the router already directly connects to both subnets once the encapsulation is correct.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You want to block guest clients from using any internal DNS servers while still allowing them to use `8.8.8.8`. The ACL is applied inbound on the guest SVI.

```text
ip access-list extended GUEST-DNS
 deny   udp 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 53
 permit udp 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 host 8.8.8.8 eq 53
 permit ip any any
!
interface Vlan50
 ip access-group GUEST-DNS in
```

What will actually happen to guest DNS traffic?
options: All guest DNS queries will be dropped, including those to 8.8.8.8.
Guests will be able to query only 8.8.8.8, as intended.
The ACL will be bypassed for DNS because UDP is stateless.
Guests can query internal DNS (e.g., 192.168.1.10) but not 8.8.8.8.
concept_mcqs.explanation: ACLs are processed top-down, first match wins. The first deny matches all guest UDP/53 traffic to any destination, so the permit for 8.8.8.8 is never reached.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B assumes ACLs evaluate all lines; they do not. C reverses the impact of the deny. D misunderstands ACL behavior; statelessness of UDP doesn’t bypass ACL processing.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A DHCP server on a router shows persistent conflicts, and users report intermittent address assignment failures.

```text
R1# show ip dhcp conflict
IP address        Detection method   Detection time       VRF
10.10.10.100      ARP                Aug 19 2026 10:11 AM --

R1# show arp | include 10.10.10.100
Internet  10.10.10.100  0   001c.73aa.bcee  ARPA  Vlan10  ; Printer (static IP)
```

Which change addresses the root cause and prevents recurrence?
options: Trust the access port with `ip dhcp snooping trust` so the offer isn’t blocked.
Exclude the printer’s IP (or static range) from the DHCP pool and then clear the conflicts.
Increase DHCP conflict detection attempts from 2 to 5 to be more certain.
Clear the DHCP conflicts so the address can be reissued immediately.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A static device is using an IP inside the pool. Excluding that address (or defining a non-overlapping pool) removes the conflict source; then clear the conflicts to recover.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B treats the symptom; the conflict will come back. C wastes time; higher detection does not fix overlapping assignments. D is unrelated; snooping trust addresses rogue servers, not overlapping pools.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Users report that some external domains with DNSSEC fail to resolve unless the resolver falls back to TCP. Firewall logs show many dropped ICMP Type 3 Code 4 packets. MTU testing shows:

```bash
# Linux test from client to Internet
ping -M do -s 1472 8.8.8.8   # OK
ping -M do -s 1473 8.8.8.8   # Frag needed and DF set (dropped by FW)
```

What change most directly fixes these DNS timeouts without disabling DNSSEC?
options: Lower the WAN interface MTU to 1200 bytes on all edge routers.
Disable EDNS0 on the resolver to force smaller DNS messages globally.
Block UDP/53 and force all DNS over TCP.
Permit ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' (Type 3 Code 4) through the firewall so PMTUD can work.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Large DNSSEC/EDNS0 responses may exceed the path MTU. Allowing ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' enables PMTUD so the sender adjusts, avoiding silent black holes.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B may mask symptoms but breaks standards and causes other issues. C is a blunt change with side effects and is unnecessary if PMTUD functions. D degrades performance and is unnecessary when path MTU issues are addressed.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After enabling DHCP snooping and IP Source Guard, a printer with a static IP on VLAN 10 lost connectivity. You must keep source guard but allow this device.

```text
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
!
interface Fa0/12
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 ip verify source
 spanning-tree portfast
!
Printer MAC: 0011.2233.4455, IP: 10.10.10.50/24
```

Which command allows this static host while maintaining source guard protections?
options:
```text
interface Fa0/12
 ip dhcp snooping trust
```

```text
ip arp timeout 60
```

```text
ip source binding 0011.2233.4455 vlan 10 10.10.10.50 interface Fa0/12
```

```text
interface Fa0/12
 no ip verify source
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: Static bindings let Source Guard validate traffic from known static hosts without disabling the protection for other ports.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B disables protection entirely on that port. C trusts DHCP messages on the port and weakens snooping; it does not create a binding for Source Guard. D changes ARP cache timing, not Source Guard validation.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your nightly config-backup script uses TFTP to pull running-configs to 10.1.1.50. Backups fail only for R1. Logs show `TFTP: error timeout`. R1 has the following ACL applied inbound on its management SVI:

```text
ip access-list extended MGMT-IN
 deny   udp any host 10.1.1.50 eq 69
 permit ip any any
!
interface Vlan99
 ip address 10.1.1.10 255.255.255.0
 ip access-group MGMT-IN in
```

What is the minimal change to restore backups for R1 without overexposing the host?
options: Insert a permit for UDP/69 to 10.1.1.50 before the deny.
Change the TFTP source-interface to Loopback0 on R1.
Permit TCP/69 to 10.1.1.50 since TFTP uses TCP.
Enable the router archive feature with `archive path tftp://10.1.1.50/$h-$t`.
concept_mcqs.explanation: TFTP uses UDP/69 on the server. The first-match ACL denies that traffic. Inserting a permit for UDP/69 to the backup server ahead of the deny allows the backup without weakening other controls.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is wrong protocol; TFTP is UDP. C does not bypass an inbound ACL on the SVI. D configures archiving but still hits the same ACL block.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your service desk uses the following priority matrix:

```text
Impact vs Urgency Matrix
- P1: Impact High (multiple services or sites) at any urgency
- P2: Impact Medium AND Urgency High
- P3: All other combinations
```

Ticket extract:

```text
Ticket: INC-4321
Title: Core switch CPU spikes every 5 minutes
Impact: High (multiple VLANs suffering jitter)
Urgency: Medium (degradation, not total outage)
Current Priority: P3
```

What should the priority be set to under this policy?
options: P2
P1
Defer to on-call engineer’s judgment instead of the matrix.
P3
concept_mcqs.explanation: High impact maps to P1 regardless of urgency by the given policy. The current P3 is incorrect.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B ignores that urgency is medium and the rule for P2 requires high urgency with medium impact. C contradicts the matrix. D circumvents the documented process.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A NAS used for nightly config archives reports the following SMART and log entries:

```text
SMART: Disk 2 pre-fail, Reallocated_Sector_Ct = 210 (threshold 140), 
Pending_Sector = 12, Last test: FAILED (read)
Backup log: Last successful full backup: 22:00 yesterday. RPO: 24h, RTO: 4h.
Maintenance policy: Replace predicted-fail disks within 48h; verify last good backup; document change; schedule during low-usage window unless risk of imminent data loss.
```

What is the best immediate next action to record in the ticket?
options: Silence the alert for 7 days and observe; SMART can be noisy.
Verify the latest backup integrity and schedule Disk 2 replacement in the next low-usage window within 48 hours.
Replace the entire NAS immediately without verifying backup, to minimize time at risk.
Run a filesystem check to clear pending sectors and defer replacement.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Policy mandates timely replacement and verification of the last good backup. Scheduling within the window respects availability targets while addressing imminent failure risk.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B ignores clear pre-fail indicators and violates policy. C risks data integrity and delays necessary replacement. D is risky without confirming a recoverable backup and may exceed RTO/RPO planning.

scenario_questions.scenario:
A small office needs a segmented network for Staff (VLAN 10) and Guest (VLAN 50). One Layer-2 switch uplinks to a router-on-a-stick gateway. A Windows DHCP/DNS server lives on the Staff VLAN (10.10.10.20). Guests must not reach the internal DNS but should reach the internet using public resolvers. There is a history of rogue DHCP servers appearing on Guest ports during events. The ISP CPE hands off a single 802.1Q trunk to your router.

You have the following constraints:
- You cannot add new hardware.
- You must preserve broadcast containment between VLANs.
- Guests should get internet via NAT, but no access to Staff hosts.
- The helpdesk must be able to understand where to place new devices and how to verify DHCP/DNS quickly.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a concrete configuration and control plan. Specify: (1) trunk/access port roles on the switch; (2) router subinterfaces and IP helper settings; (3) DHCP snooping and trust/binding placements; (4) ACLs to enforce Guest DNS policy and block inter-VLAN access while allowing necessary gateway services; (5) at least three verification commands or tests the helpdesk can run. Justify each choice briefly.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
- Switch: Access ports for Staff assigned to VLAN 10; access ports for Guest assigned to VLAN 50; uplink to router as 802.1Q trunk allowing VLANs 10,50; enable portfast on access ports.
- Router: g0/0.10 encaps dot1Q 10, IP 10.10.10.1/24; g0/0.50 encaps dot1Q 50, IP 10.50.50.1/24; configure `ip helper-address 10.10.10.20` on subinterface for VLAN 50 only so Guest DHCP relays to the Windows server; no helper on VLAN 10 since the server is local; NAT overload on WAN.
- DHCP snooping: Enable globally and on VLANs 10 and 50; trust the trunk uplink to the router and the server-facing Staff switchport; all Guest access ports untrusted; enable `ip source guard` on Guest ports; optionally add static bindings for known static hosts.
- ACLs: Inbound on Vlan50 SVI deny udp 192.168.50.0/24 to any eq 53; then explicitly permit udp to 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 eq 53; then permit ip to gateway IPs (e.g., allow to 10.50.50.1 for ARP/ICMP as needed); finally deny ip 10.50.50.0/24 to 10.10.10.0/24; allow ip any any for rest to reach NAT. Alternatively apply an outbound ACL on Vlan50 to enforce the same order with the specific permits above the denies.
- Verification: `show vlan brief` and `show interfaces trunk` on the switch; `show ip dhcp snooping`, `show ip dhcp snooping binding`; test `ipconfig /renew` on Guest; packet capture or `debug ip dhcp server packet` to verify relayed DHCP; `nslookup` on Guest to confirm public resolvers; ping Staff host from Guest should fail; ping gateway and internet from Guest should succeed.
- Justifications: Helper on Guest only avoids leaking Staff broadcasts; snooping prevents rogue DHCP on Guest; ACL order avoids shadowing specific DNS permits; trunk design preserves VLAN separation while enabling routing at the router.

rubric.criterion: Correct port-role plan (access VLANs for Staff/Guest, trunk to router) and preservation of broadcast domains
Router subinterfaces and correct placement of IP helper (on Guest only) with correct gateway IPs
Appropriate DHCP snooping deployment (trusted/untrusted delineation, mention of Source Guard or bindings)
ACL design that enforces Guest DNS to public servers and blocks Guest-to-Staff while allowing necessary traffic; correct ordering rationale
At least three concrete verification commands/tests tied to the design

scenario_questions.scenario: After a change, Staff hosts can resolve internal names like `files.corp.local` but some external SaaS domains intermittently fail to resolve or resolve to internal addresses. The Windows DNS server is configured for split-brain DNS with a corp.local authoritative zone and conditional forwarders. Recent change log: "Added conditional forwarder for external.com to 10.10.10.20 (internal proxy/DNS)". Users report `www.external.com` sometimes resolves to 10.10.10.30 (an internal reverse proxy) rather than the public IP. Internet browsing from Guest VLAN is unaffected.
scenario_questions.task: Identify the most likely misconfiguration and propose a corrective plan with justification. Include: (1) what is wrong; (2) the specific DNS configuration changes; (3) how to verify the fix and avoid regression (monitoring/logging).
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
(1) The conditional forwarder for external.com points to an internal resolver that rewrites or resolves internal hostnames for that domain (e.g., proxy split-horizon), causing internal addresses to leak into general Staff resolution. Forwarding for an external public domain to an internal rewriting resolver is misapplied.
(2) Remove or correct the conditional forwarder: point external.com to public resolvers or the ISP recursive resolvers; or remove it entirely to use normal recursion. Ensure the authoritative corp.local zone remains intact and that no wildcard or stub zones shadow external.com. If internal access to `external.com` via reverse proxy is required, create specific internal host overrides (e.g., `proxy.external.com`) rather than blanket forwarding that returns internal IPs.
(3) Verification: Clear server and client caches; `nslookup/dig external.com` and `www.external.com` from multiple VLANs should return public IPs; query `nslookup -type=ns external.com` to confirm delegation to public NS; enable Windows DNS query logging and set up alerts for answers in RFC1918 ranges for non-internal zones; document the change in the runbook and change log.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies the conditional forwarder to an internal rewriting resolver as the root cause
Proposes precise DNS changes (remove/retarget forwarder; avoid zone shadowing; specific overrides if needed)
Verification steps including cache clear and specific queries that prove public resolution; monitoring/logging plan to prevent regression

scenario_questions.scenario: A distribution switch lost its running-config after a power event and rebooted with factory defaults. The site was down until someone consoled in and reapplied a weeks-old config from a USB stick. There is currently an ad-hoc TFTP backup script on a laptop that may or may not run nightly.
scenario_questions.task: Design a resilient configuration-backup and recovery workflow for network devices that fits a small environment with no extra paid tools. Include: (1) trigger and schedule; (2) transport/protocols; (3) secure storage layout and retention; (4) verification of backups and periodic restore testing; (5) tie-ins to ticketing and documentation.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
(1) Schedule nightly backups via device `archive` feature or EEM applets at staggered times, triggered by config changes (archive write-memory) and a nightly cron on a central Linux host to pull via SCP.
(2) Use SCP or SFTP over SSH for transport (avoid TFTP on shared networks). Lock device management ACLs to the backup server. Optionally use RANCID/Oxidized (free) for versioning via Git.
(3) Store per-device directories with timestamped filenames; encrypt at rest (filesystem encryption) and restrict permissions; keep 30 daily, 12 monthly; mirror to NAS with SMART monitoring.
(4) After each run, parse logs and verify file sizes and config headers; weekly sample test: load a backup into a lab device or diff against running-config; maintain a golden baseline and alert on drift.
(5) Create a recurring maintenance ticket for backup success checks; auto-attach logs; document recovery steps (console access, copy tftp/scp start, verify VLANs, SVIs, ACLs); update network diagram and inventory with management IPs and backup statuses.

rubric.criterion: Clear schedule/triggers covering both nightly cadence and on-change archiving
Appropriate secure transport and access controls (SSH/SCP, management ACLs), avoiding insecure defaults
Storage organization, permissions, retention, and redundancy details
Verification and periodic restore-testing approach that would actually detect bad backups
Integration with ticketing/documentation (evidence, runbooks, change logs)

scenario_questions.scenario: Your org wants a preventive maintenance program that reduces outages from avoidable causes (dusty racks, aging UPS batteries, hot switch closets, stale firmware on routers). The team uses a basic ITSM tool with custom fields and SLA timers. You cannot exceed 4 engineer-hours per month on routine checks across two sites.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a quarterly preventive maintenance checklist and a ticketing workflow that fits the time budget and produces auditable evidence. Include concrete checks (what to measure/collect), pass/fail thresholds, escalation rules, and how to attach evidence. Explain how this reduces incidents without creating busywork.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Checklist (quarterly, with monthly quick checks limited to key sensors):
- Environmentals: record closet temp/humidity; thresholds 18–27°C, <60% RH; attach photos of thermostat and sensor exports; escalate P1 if >30°C sustained.
- Power: UPS status and battery age; run a self-test off-hours; threshold: any battery >36 months or self-test fail -> create change for replacement; attach screenshots/log exports.
- Hardware health: fan/PSU LEDs, error counters (`show env`, `show power`, SMART on NAS); threshold: any warning -> incident ticket plus vendor RMA if needed; attach CLI outputs.
- Backups: verify last 7 nightly successes and size variance <10%; threshold: 2 consecutive failures -> incident; attach logs and diff summary.
- Firmware: check against approved baseline; if outdated and security-relevant, raise change ticket with vendor release notes attached.
- Housekeeping: rack cleanliness, cable strain relief; attach dated photos; threshold: any obstructed airflow -> work order.
Workflow:
- Create a recurring “PM-Quarterly” ticket with subtasks per check; timebox per site to 2 hours; auto-templates for evidence fields and required attachments.
- SLA: PM ticket due within 10 business days of quarter start; subtasks failing thresholds auto-spawn incidents/changes with correct priority.
- Evidence: upload photos, CLI outputs, exported logs; add sign-off checklist; store links to config-backup repo snapshot.
Impact: Early detection (thermal, power, failing disks) reduces surprise outages; attaching objective evidence avoids subjectivity and supports audits while keeping within the 4-hour cap.

rubric.criterion: Concrete checklist with measurable items and realistic thresholds tied to network hardware/support scope
Time-bounded workflow using ticketing with subtasks and evidence requirements
Clear escalation rules mapping threshold breaches to incident/change tickets
Explanation of how plan reduces incidents without busywork

practical_tasks.title: Build and validate a two-VLAN small network with routed gateway, DHCP relay, DNS policy, and basic switch security
practical_tasks.brief: Assemble a lab (Packet Tracer/GNS3 or physical) with one router (or L3 switch), one access switch, a DHCP/DNS server, and two PCs. Implement VLAN 10 (Staff) and VLAN 50 (Guest). Provide inter-VLAN routing at the router, DHCP for both VLANs (server on VLAN 10, helper for VLAN 50), block Guest access to Staff, and allow Guest DNS only to public resolvers. Add basic Layer-2 security: enable DHCP snooping on both VLANs (trust only uplinks/server port) and IP Source Guard on Guest access ports. Validate with commands and end-to-end tests.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A zipped folder containing: (1) topology diagram (PNG/PDF) and IP plan (text/CSV); (2) device configuration files (router and switch running-configs); (3) DHCP server scope configuration or screenshots; (4) validation outputs: `show vlan`, `show interfaces trunk`, `show ip dhcp snooping`, `show ip dhcp snooping binding`, ACL hits/counters, and PC-side `ipconfig`/`nslookup`/`ping` transcripts demonstrating policy; (5) a one-page runbook describing where to plug new devices and how to verify DHCP/DNS.
acceptance_criteria: Diagram shows router-on-a-stick (or L3 SVI) with VLANs 10 and 50, labeled ports, and correct addressing.
Router has working subinterfaces/SVIs with correct IPs; VLAN 50 uses `ip helper-address` pointing to the server in VLAN 10; DHCP leases obtained on both VLANs.
Switch access ports assigned to correct VLANs; trunk between switch and router carries VLANs 10 and 50; portfast enabled on access ports.
Guest-to-Staff isolation enforced (ping from Guest to Staff host fails; ping/HTTP to internet simulated succeeds).
DNS policy enforced for Guest: queries to internal DNS blocked; queries to allowed public resolver succeed; ACL counters reflect matches.
DHCP snooping enabled on both VLANs; only uplink/server-facing port trusted; Source Guard enabled on Guest access ports; bindings table shows dynamic Guest entries.
Submission includes all requested configs and validation outputs; commands are reproducible and clearly labeled.

rubric.criterion: Correct L2/L3 design and configs (VLANs, trunk, SVIs/subinterfaces, helper) that produce working routing and DHCP
Guest-to-Staff isolation and DNS policy implemented with correctly ordered ACLs and evidence of effect
DHCP snooping and Source Guard correctly deployed with appropriate trust/binding and evidence
Quality of documentation: clear diagram, IP plan, and concise runbook for helpdesk use
Complete, labeled validation evidence demonstrating each acceptance criterion

practical_tasks.title: Complete support lab: documentation, automated config backups, ticket workflow, and preventive maintenance evidence
practical_tasks.brief: Create a lightweight, auditable support lab demonstrating core support operations. Use two network devices (simulated or real), a Linux VM as backup server, and your existing lab from Task 1. Implement automated nightly configuration backups over SCP, with retention and integrity checks. Produce operator-facing documentation for the environment. Demonstrate ticket handling for an incident and for a preventive maintenance cycle, including evidence attachments and SLA fields.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A zipped folder containing: (1) a network documentation pack: updated topology, IP plan, device inventory with management addresses, and a change/runbook (PDF/markdown); (2) backup configuration: device archive/SCP settings, Linux cron job and script files, and last run logs; (3) a sample restore test transcript showing a config pulled from backup and compared/applied on a device (lab-safe); (4) ticket exports (PDF/CSV/screenshots) for one incident (e.g., DHCP failure) and one PM ticket with subtasks, timestamps, and attached evidence (photos/CLI/logs); (5) a preventive maintenance checklist with filled results for the lab.
acceptance_criteria: Documentation pack includes topology, IP plan, inventory, and runbook; all fields populated and consistent with configs.
Automated backups run via SCP from devices or pull from server; cron entries and scripts included; credentials handled securely (no plaintext in docs; use SSH keys or redaction).
Backup logs show at least two device configs captured with timestamps; retention policy documented; files organized per-device; permissions or notes on secure storage included.
Restore test shows retrieval of a saved config and a comparison to running-config (diff or show commands) and a safe application plan.
Tickets show correct categorization, priorities per a stated matrix, status progression, and attached evidence (logs/CLI outputs/screenshots).
Preventive maintenance checklist includes concrete checks, thresholds, results, and spawned follow-up tickets where thresholds exceeded.

rubric.criterion: Completeness and quality of documentation set (diagram, IP plan, inventory, runbook) and consistency with the lab
Working automated backup pipeline over secure transport with clear scheduling, retention, and secure handling
Convincing restore verification procedure and evidence (diff or test apply)
Ticket workflow quality: correct use of fields, priority matrix adherence, evidence attachments, lifecycle
Preventive maintenance checklist with results and appropriate follow-up tickets
